title: Motorbike rental in HCMC: prices, deposit and papers (2026)
description: Ho Chi Minh City motorbike rental prices by bike, delivery, a fair deposit, the ID-card rule, the papers and fines, and what to do after a crash in the city.
h1: Renting a motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City: prices, deposits and what to check before you ride off
intro: Renting a motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City costs least for a manual Wave Alpha, most for a Honda SH, and far less by the month, according to a 25 September 2026 list on the travel site vietnamtourism.com. Some shops deliver within the city for a fee. You need an A1 licence for bikes up to 125 cc, plus the shop's registration paper and insurance certificate. Pay a cash deposit instead of leaving your ID card, film the bike before riding off, and after a crash stop, help, call 113 or 115 and tell the shop.
keyPoints: According to the travel site vietnamtourism.com (25 September 2026), a Wave Alpha in Saigon costs {{vnd:90000-120000}} a day, a Honda Vision {{vnd:120000-150000}}, an Air Blade {{vnd:150000-180000}} and a Honda SH {{vnd:250000-350000}}. Fuel is not included, and delivery within the city costs about {{vnd:50000-100000}} at shops that charge for it.
Monthly hire is much cheaper: a Vision runs {{vnd:1500000-1800000}} a month and an Air Blade {{vnd:1800000-2200000}} a month, according to the same list.

Leave a cash deposit, not your documents. The same source suggests {{vnd:2000000-5000000}} and calls anything above {{vnd:5000000}} for an ordinary bike a red flag. Pawning a Vietnamese ID card is banned by law.

After a crash the law says stop, keep the scene as it is, help anyone hurt and stay until the police arrive. You may leave only for emergency care or if your own life or health is threatened, and must then report to the nearest police straight away (Article 80, Law 36/2024/QH15).
Bikes up to 125 cc need an **A1** licence; above 125 cc needs an **A** licence. Riding a bike up to 125 cc with no licence is fined {{vnd:2000000-4000000}}.
You must carry the bike's **registration certificate** and the **compulsory civil liability insurance certificate**, so get both from the shop before you leave.

sections.title: How much does it cost to rent a motorbike in HCMC?

blocks.text: A manual Wave Alpha is the cheapest bike to rent in Ho Chi Minh City and a Honda SH the most expensive. Monthly rates cost a fraction of paying day by day. The figures below come from a reference price list for Saigon that the travel site vietnamtourism.com updated on 25 September 2026. Every shop sets its own prices, so use the list to judge whether a quote is fair, not as a fixed tariff.

blocks.caption: Reference motorbike rental prices in Ho Chi Minh City, according to the travel site vietnamtourism.com, updated 25 September 2026; fuel, raincoat and delivery not included

blocks.text: Extras come on top. According to [the travel site vietnamtourism.com](https://www.vietnamtourism.com/vi/thue-xe-may-theo-thang-o-sai-gon-bang-gia-moi-nhat-va-cach-c) (September 2026), some shops charge **{{vnd:50000-100000}} to deliver the bike** within the inner city, and a raincoat costs {{vnd:10000-20000}} if hired separately. The same page says helmets usually come free but are often poor quality. It suggests buying your own for about {{vnd:150000-300000}}, for example along Bùi Viện or at Chợ Nhật Tảo.

The same page treats a price far below the list as a warning sign: it cites an Air Blade offered at {{vnd:800000}} a month. Before you agree, ask what the price covers, what late return costs, and how much fuel the shop expects in the tank when you bring the bike back.

blocks.title: Ask for the monthly rate first
blocks.text: If you need a bike for more than a couple of weeks, ask for the monthly price straight away. On the list above, a month on an Air Blade costs about the same as 12 separate days.

sections.title: Where to rent: searching "thue xe may tphcm"

blocks.text: Most rental shops in Ho Chi Minh City advertise in Vietnamese, so searching **thuê xe máy TP.HCM** (typed as "thue xe may tphcm") turns up far more local shops than an English search. Thuê xe máy means motorbike rental, and TP.HCM is the Vietnamese abbreviation for Ho Chi Minh City.

On eno.vn, you can browse the [motorbike rental listings for Ho Chi Minh City](/motorbike-rental-ho-chi-minh-city), the [motorbike rental listings in Vietnamese](/thue-xe-may-tphcm) and [vehicles for sale or hire](/c/vehicles). Wherever you rent, the deposit, paperwork and checks below still apply.

If the shop delivers, do the checks below on your doorstep before the driver leaves, and pay the deposit only against a signed receipt. Renting outside the city or riding between provinces is covered in [our guide to renting a motorbike across Vietnam](/guides/renting-a-motorbike-in-vietnam).

sections.title: How much deposit, and should you leave your passport or ID card?

blocks.text: No law sets the deposit amount, so each shop decides. A guide on the travel site vietnamtourism.com, updated 25 September 2026, suggests a **cash deposit of {{vnd:2000000-5000000}}** instead of handing over your original passport. The same guide calls a deposit above {{vnd:5000000}} for an ordinary bike a warning sign.

For Vietnamese citizens, the law is on your side. The 2023 Law on Identification bans renting out, pawning or accepting a pawned ID card (thẻ căn cước) and bans holding someone's card unlawfully. According to [Tạp chí Luật sư Việt Nam](https://lsvn.vn/tang-muc-phat-voi-cac-vi-pham-lien-quan-den-can-cuoc-a165531.html) (5 November 2025), Decree 282/2025/ND-CP replaced Decree 144/2021/ND-CP from 15 December 2025. Under Article 11(4) of Decree 282/2025/ND-CP, pawning an ID card, or accepting one in pawn, is fined {{vnd:8000000-10000000}}. Offer the shop a photo or photocopy of your ID and pay the deposit in cash.

items: For a bank transfer, write a clear reference, for example: bike deposit, plate number, pick-up date.
For cash, get a signed receipt showing the amount and when you get it back.
Ask up front when the deposit comes back, what can be deducted from it, and who pays for repairs caused by normal wear.

sections.title: What to do after an accident on a rented motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City

blocks.text: Stop, help anyone injured, call for help and stay until the police arrive. [Article 80 of Law 36/2024/QH15](https://hethongphapluat.com/luat-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-duong-bo-2024/dieu-80) puts these duties on any driver involved. You may leave only if you are injured and need emergency care, to take an injured person for emergency care, or if your own life or health is threatened. Anyone who leaves must report straight away to the nearest police or People's Committee. Leaving the scene for any other reason makes everything after it harder, including the insurance claim.

items.title: Stop and warn others
items.text: Stop immediately, warn traffic behind you, keep the scene as it is and help anyone hurt.

items.title: Call for help
items.text: Call **115** for an ambulance and **113** for the police. According to [VOH](https://voh.com.vn/xa-hoi/112-tro-thanh-so-dien-thoai-khan-cap-quoc-gia-619717.html), **112** is the national emergency number, calls to it are free, and it passes calls straight on to 113, 114 or 115.

items.title: Stay at the scene
items.text: The law requires you to stay until the police arrive and to give them information that identifies you. The only exceptions are emergency care for you or an injured person, or a threat to your own life or health; then report to the nearest police straight away.

items.title: Take photos and notes
items.text: Photograph where the vehicles are, the plates, the damage and the road surface. Ask witnesses for a phone number if they are willing.

items.title: Tell the rental shop straight away
items.text: According to CafeF (28 July 2026), a compulsory-insurance claim needs a written claim request, the registration certificate, the rider's licence and ID, and the insurance certificate. Some of these belong to the bike's owner, so you need the shop's cooperation.

items.title: Don't sign or pay in a hurry
items.text: Don't sign anything accepting full blame while fault is unclear. Agree compensation only with the police present or with the agreement written down.

blocks.text: The compulsory insurance under Decree 67/2023/ND-CP is **civil liability cover for harm to other people**. According to [CafeF (28 July 2026)](https://cafef.vn/tat-ca-nguoi-dan-dang-di-xe-may-chu-y-muc-boi-thuong-bao-hiem-bat-buoc-moi-nhat-2026-188260728055117848.chn), injury payouts follow the decree's injury table. Property payouts follow the actual damage and each rider's share of fault, up to the insurer's limit. Damage to the rented bike itself is usually governed by your rental agreement, so settle that before you take the bike.

blocks.title: The most common mistake
blocks.text: After a minor crash, renters often push the bike back to the shop and only then report it. By then there is no police record and no scene, and the shop can take the whole repair bill from your deposit. Call the police and the shop from the scene.
If you need a doctor afterwards, see [healthcare and health insurance in Ho Chi Minh City](/teach-in-vietnam/healthcare-and-health-insurance-in-ho-chi-minh-city).

sections.title: Which licence and papers you need to ride a rented bike

blocks.text: You need an A1 licence for a bike up to 125 cc and an A licence above that. While riding you must carry the bike's registration certificate, your licence and the compulsory insurance certificate. This comes from the Law on Road Traffic Order and Safety (Law 36/2024/QH15), which took effect on 1 January 2025 and applies across Vietnam. Under [Article 57](https://hethongphapluat.com/luat-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-duong-bo-2024/khoan-1-dieu-57), **class A1** covers motorbikes up to 125 cm3 or electric motors up to 11 kW, and **class A** covers anything above.

items: A Vision, a 125 cc Air Blade or a Wave needs only A1. For anything bigger, check the engine size printed on the registration certificate.

The Honda SH is sold in Vietnam as the SH125i and the SH160i, according to [CafeF](https://cafef.vn/xe-tay-ga-honda-sh-ban-tai-viet-nam-duoc-nang-cap-188261028072337995.chn) (28 October 2026). The 160 cc versions are above 125 cm3 and need **class A** on a new licence, so check the engine size on the registration certificate before you rent an SH.

**Licences issued before 1 January 2025** stay valid until the expiry date printed on them. An old A1 licence that has not been exchanged still covers bikes from 50 cm3 up to under 175 cm3 (Article 89).

You must be 18 to get an A1 licence. Mopeds (xe gắn máy) may be ridden from 16 (Article 59). Under Article 34, a moped is a vehicle with a design speed of no more than 50 km/h and, with a petrol engine, up to 50 cm3, or with an electric motor, up to 4 kW.

blocks.text: [Article 56](https://hethongphapluat.com/luat-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-duong-bo-2024/dieu-56) lists what you must carry: the **vehicle registration certificate**, the **licence** for that class of vehicle, and the **compulsory civil liability insurance certificate**. Documents linked to an electronic identification account (VNeID) can be shown that way instead. Your licence may be in your own VNeID, but a rented bike is registered to its owner, so you still need its papers from the shop.

The law mentions a certified copy of the registration only when the bike is mortgaged to a lender, and then together with the lender's original confirmation. Many shops hand over a plain photocopy. Ask exactly which paper they are giving you, and who pays the fine if police stop you over it.

blocks.caption: Selected fines for motorbike riders under Decree 168/2024/ND-CP, as summarised by Tạp chí Luật sư Việt Nam on 22 February 2026, with the confiscation condition from the text of Article 14
rows: No licence, bike up to 125 cm3
{{vnd:2000000-3000000}}, 2 licence points deducted; the bike may be confiscated if its origin cannot be proven

blocks.text: A rider who cannot show the registration when stopped, on paper or in VNeID, is written up as having **no registration** under [Article 48(3) of Decree 168/2024/ND-CP](https://hethongphapluat.com/nghi-dinh-168-2024-nd-cp-quy-dinh-xu-phat-vi-pham-hanh-chinh-ve-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-trong-linh-vuc-giao-thong-duong-bo-tru-diem-phuc-hoi-diem-giay-phep-lai-xe/dieu-48): {{vnd:2000000-3000000}} and 2 licence points ([Art 14(2)(a) and (8)(a)](https://hethongphapluat.com/nghi-dinh-168-2024-nd-cp-quy-dinh-xu-phat-vi-pham-hanh-chinh-ve-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-trong-linh-vuc-giao-thong-duong-bo-tru-diem-phuc-hoi-diem-giay-phep-lai-xe/dieu-14)), and the bike may be held. Under Article 48(3)(c), that fine is dropped if the papers are shown by the deadline written in the report.

Decree 238/2026/ND-CP amended parts of Decree 168 from 15 August 2026. According to [CafeF](https://cafef.vn/quy-dinh-moi-ve-xu-phat-vi-pham-giao-thong-ap-dung-tu-ngay-15-8-tat-ca-nguoi-dan-chu-y-188260730065435832.chn), the motorbike change concerns riders aged 16 to under 18. The article does not mention the offences in the table above. If you are being fined for a specific offence, the penalty decision itself is what counts.

To ride with a foreign licence, you need a Vietnamese licence covering the bike, a licence from an ASEAN country covering it, or an international driving permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention, carried together with a home licence that covers motorcycles ([Article 57](https://hethongphapluat.com/luat-trat-tu-an-toan-giao-thong-duong-bo-2024/dieu-57)). A licence from an ASEAN country counts only for a short stay: it is recognised under the [1985 ASEAN Agreement on the recognition of domestic driving licences](https://cil.nus.edu.sg/database/single-database/?id=53508), and according to [Tuoi Tre News](https://news.tuoitre.vn/can-a-drivers-license-issued-in-indonesia-be-used-in-vietnam-10326060311084772.htm) (3 June 2026) that arrangement is meant for travel and short stays, not for living in Vietnam long term without exchanging the licence. According to [the travel site vietnamtourism.com](https://www.vietnamtourism.com/en/international-driving-permit-for-motorbikes-in-vietnam-what-your-license-really-covers) (30 October 2026), permits issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention are not valid in Vietnam. [Vietcetera](https://vietcetera.com/en/why-many-foreigners-ride-illegally-in-vietnam-without-realizing-it) names the US and Canada among the countries that issue that older permit. For the details, read [the motorbike licence guide for foreigners](/teach-in-vietnam/motorbike-licence-in-vietnam-for-foreigners) before you rent.

sections.title: What to check on the bike before you ride off

blocks.text: Most disputes at return are about scratches and faults that were already there. Ten minutes of checks and a video at pick-up protect your deposit.

items.title: Film the whole bike
items.text: Walk slowly round the bike with the shop in shot. Film the scratches, the dashboard (odometer and fuel gauge) and the plate up close. Send the video to the shop by message so it carries a timestamp.

items.title: Match the papers
items.text: The plate and frame number must match the registration certificate. Check the expiry date on the insurance certificate.

items.title: Test brakes, lights and horn
items.text: Try each brake at walking pace. Check high and low beam, both indicators and the brake light, then sound the horn.

items.title: Look at the tyres and the chain or belt
items.text: Bald, cracked or soft tyres are a reason to ask for another bike. In the rainy season, tyres and brakes matter even more.

items.title: Check mirrors, stand and steering lock
items.text: Both mirrors should be firm and the stand should spring back up. Take every key, including the seat or storage key.

items.title: Get a helmet and raincoat
items.text: The helmet must fit and the strap must fasten. Ask whether the raincoat costs extra.

blocks.text: What to put in the rental agreement

items: Price, pick-up and return times, and the late fee.
Deposit amount, when it comes back, and what can be deducted.
Who pays for wear-and-tear repairs and who pays for crash damage.
What happens if the bike is stolen or impounded.
A phone number to call if the bike breaks down on the road.

sections.title: When another way of getting around makes more sense

blocks.text: If you don't hold the right licence class, aren't used to rush-hour traffic, or only need a few trips, ride-hailing or Metro Line 1 (Ben Thanh to Suoi Tien) may cost less and carry less risk. The options are compared in [getting around Ho Chi Minh City](/teach-in-vietnam/getting-around-ho-chi-minh-city). For groups or longer trips, look at [car rental in Ho Chi Minh City](/car-rental-ho-chi-minh-city).

faqs.q: How much is it to rent a motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City per day?
faqs.a: Motorbike rental in Ho Chi Minh City depends on the bike. According to a 25 September 2026 list on the travel site vietnamtourism.com, a manual Wave Alpha is the cheapest, Honda Vision and Air Blade scooters sit in the middle, and a Honda SH costs roughly three times as much as a Wave. Fuel, raincoat hire and delivery are extra. The exact daily and monthly ranges are in the price table on this page.

faqs.q: Can I rent a motorbike in HCMC without a licence?
faqs.a: Some shops in Ho Chi Minh City will rent a motorbike to anyone, but the rider pays the fine, not the shop. Under Article 18 of Decree 168/2024/ND-CP, riding a motorbike without a licence is fined, and the fine is higher for bikes over 125 cc. A moped needs no licence: it has a design speed of no more than 50 km/h and up to 50 cm3 with a petrol engine or up to 4 kW with an electric motor. The rider must be at least 16. Mopeds are rare in rental shops.

faqs.q: Can I ride a rented motorbike in Vietnam with an international driving permit?
faqs.a: An international driving permit is valid in Vietnam only if it was issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention and is carried together with a home licence that covers motorcycles, under Article 57 of Law 36/2024/QH15. A Vietnamese licence covering the bike also works, and so does a licence from an ASEAN country, but only for a short stay under the 1985 ASEAN Agreement on driving licences. Permits issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention, such as those from the US and Canada, are not valid in Vietnam.

faqs.q: Can an old A1 licence ride a 150cc scooter in Vietnam?
faqs.a: Yes. An A1 licence issued before 1 January 2025 that has not been exchanged still covers two-wheelers from 50 cm3 up to under 175 cm3, under Article 89 of the Law on Road Traffic Order and Safety. A new A1 licence issued under the current law covers only bikes up to 125 cm3. A 150 cc scooter on a new licence needs class A.

faqs.q: What does thue xe may tphcm mean?
faqs.a: Thuê xe máy TP.HCM is Vietnamese for motorbike rental in Ho Chi Minh City. Thuê means rent, xe máy means motorbike, and TP.HCM is the short form of Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh. Searching thue xe may tphcm finds many more local rental shops than English searches do, because most shops advertise only in Vietnamese.

faqs.q: Should I leave my passport as a deposit for a motorbike rental in Saigon?
faqs.a: Leaving a passport as a deposit is best avoided. A September 2026 guide on the travel site vietnamtourism.com suggests a cash deposit instead and treats a very high deposit for an ordinary bike as a warning sign. For Vietnamese citizens, the 2023 Law on Identification bans pawning ID cards and holding them unlawfully. Get a signed receipt for any cash deposit.

faqs.q: Who pays if a rented motorbike is stolen in Ho Chi Minh City?
faqs.a: No law sets a standard payout for a stolen rental motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City. Responsibility depends on what the rental agreement says, so put it in writing before you take the bike. If the motorbike is stolen, report it to the police straight away and get written confirmation, then tell the rental shop.
